body.statement: The algorithm \(\mathsf{ChamberMax}\) computes \(P_\delta(a)\) and an optimizing weak-order certificate using at most \(\prod_{j=0}^{k-1}\{2(g+j)+1\}\le(2n+1)^k\) leaves and \(O((2n+1)^k nL\,\operatorname{poly}(\ell))\) bit operations. For \(k=1\), an equality-inclusive sweep through the \(2g+1\) positions runs in \(O(nL\,\operatorname{poly}(\ell))\) after sorting. This is an \(\mathrm{XP}\), not an \(\mathrm{FPT}\), guarantee.
body.justification: The bound locates the exact tractable regime and gives a sharp practical routine when attrition is small.
body.gap: Sills computes a fixed tied-rank distribution, and Mehta, Patel, and Wei exploit special design recursions; neither enumerates completion weak orders for a supplied weighted support.
body.consumer: Small-attrition cluster trials can compute the exact robust p-value rather than use Monte Carlo completion searches.
body.proof_tex:
Begin with the \(g\) ordered equality blocks of the observed coordinates.  Process the \(k\) missing labels in a fixed label order.  If the current ordered partition has \(h\) blocks, the next label can either be inserted as a singleton in one of the \(h+1\) gaps or attached to one of the \(h\) blocks.  These \(2h+1\) choices are exhaustive and mutually exclusive.

The insertion is reversible.  In a final partition, remove the last processed missing label: if its block contains another label, the last operation was attachment to that block; if it is a singleton block, the last operation was insertion in the uniquely determined adjacent gap.  Induction on the number of processed labels therefore shows that every compatible final weak order is produced exactly once.  After \(j\) insertions there are at most \(g+j\) blocks.  Thus the number of leaves is at most
\[
C(g,k)=\prod_{j=0}^{k-1}\{2(g+j)+1\}.
\]
The empty product is one when \(k=0\).  Since \(g+j\le n\),
\[
C(g,k)\le(2n+1)^k.
\]

At a leaf, scan the ordered blocks.  A block of size \(d\) preceded by \(c\) labels has doubled rank \(2c+d+1\).  Thus all doubled ranks are integers of magnitude at most \(2n\).  For every listed row \(z\), compute \(2T(z,b)=\sum_i z_i\,2r_i(b)\), compare it with \(2T(a,b)\), and add the corresponding exact rational weight.  This costs \(O(nL)\) arithmetic operations per leaf.  The weak-order-attainment theorem shows that maximizing these leaf values computes exactly \(P_\delta(a)\), and its rational-representative construction converts the retained ordered partition into an optimizing certificate.

For bit complexity, the rational input comparisons used in the initial sort have polynomial cost in \(\ell\).  A common denominator for all listed weights has binary length no larger than the sum of their encoded denominator lengths, which is \(O(\ell)\).  Tail sums can therefore be accumulated as integers of polynomial binary length; doubled rank sums have \(O(\log n)\) bits.  The insertion tree has depth \(k\le n\), so its bookkeeping is absorbed by the leaf evaluation bound.  Consequently the total cost is
\[
O\!\left((2n+1)^k nL\,\operatorname{poly}(\ell)\right),
\]
after sorting, as claimed.  For each fixed \(k\) this is polynomial, but the displayed exponent depends on \(k\), so the conclusion is \(\mathrm{XP}\), not \(\mathrm{FPT}\).

For \(k=1\), let \(u\) be the missing label and let \(B_1,\ldots,B_g\) be the observed blocks from bottom to top.  There are exactly \(g+1\) strict gaps and \(g\) equality positions, hence \(2g+1\) positions.  Put
\[
d_i(z)=z_i-a_i,
\qquad
D_z= T(z,b)-T(a,b)=\sum_i d_i(z)r_i(b).
\]
When \(u\) moves from immediately below an observed block \(B\) of size \(t\) onto its equality face, \(r_u\) increases by \(t/2\), while each rank in \(B\) decreases by \(1/2\).  Therefore
\[
D_z(\text{face})-D_z(\text{lower gap})
=\frac{t,d_u(z)-\sum_{i\in B}d_i(z)}{2}.
\]
Exactly the same increment takes the equality face to the upper gap.  Precomputing every block sum for all \(z\in\Omega\) and initializing all \(D_z\) costs \(O(nL)\).  Each of the \(2g\) half-steps and each exact weighted-tail evaluation then costs \(O(L)\).  Since \(g\le n\), the complete equality-inclusive sweep costs \(O(nL\operatorname{poly}(\ell))\) after sorting.
